# Sadhaka — opensadhaka.com

> Sadhaka is an English-language reference for Sanatan Dharma — the philosophies, texts, practices, and living traditions of the Indian spiritual inheritance. Content covers Vedanta (Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita), Shaiva, Shakta, and Vaishnava traditions, sacred texts (Vedas, Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, Puranas), stotras and sahasranamas, Jyotish, Sanskrit vocabulary, and contemporary bridges to philosophy and psychology.

Canonical site: https://www.opensadhaka.com
Editorial standards: https://www.opensadhaka.com/about
License: Editorial content © Sadhaka. Quotation with attribution and a link back to the source URL is permitted. Canonical Sanskrit primary sources (Vedas, Upanishads, Gita) are in the public domain.

## Editorial articles

In-depth essays on Sanatan philosophy, practices, and modern bridges. Each article has a direct-answer opening, inline citations from primary texts, and a FAQ block.

- [How to Start Japa: Mantra, Mala, Method (Beginner Guide)](https://www.opensadhaka.com/how-to-start-japa): Krishna called japa the highest sacrifice (BG 10.25). Choose a mantra, learn the 3 levels of practice (vaikhari, upamshu, manasika), use a mala correctly, and avoid the one mistake most beginners make.
- [Bhagavad Gita Complete Guide: Chapters, Teachings, and How to Read It](https://www.opensadhaka.com/bhagavad-gita-complete-guide): Bhagavad Gita complete guide for serious beginners: its 18 chapters, 700 verses, core yogas, Arjuna's crisis, and how to read the text without flattening it into battlefield motivation.
- [Spiritual Practice Sequence: The Graded Curriculum from the Gita, Yoga Sutras & Shankara](https://www.opensadhaka.com/spiritual-practice-sequence): Indian spiritual practice is a graded curriculum, not a buffet. The Gita, Yoga Sutras, and Shankara's sadhana chatushtaya prescribe practices in order of readiness. Learn the sequence.
- [Spiritual Paths Explained: Inquiry, Devotion, Discipline, and Ritual](https://www.opensadhaka.com/spiritual-paths-explained): Spiritual paths explained through the Bhagavad Gita's fourfold framework: Karma, Bhakti, Jnana, and Dhyana, how temperaments differ, and why not every path fits every seeker equally well.
- [Indian Philosophy vs Western Philosophy: The Vedanta Bridge](https://www.opensadhaka.com/western-philosophy-and-vedanta): Indian philosophy vs western philosophy: clear differences, core convergences, and how Vedanta reframes consciousness, ethics, and meaning for modern seekers.
- [Vedanta vs Stoicism: Similar Discipline, Different Metaphysics](https://www.opensadhaka.com/vedanta-vs-stoicism): Vedanta vs Stoicism explained: where they converge on discipline and detachment, where they differ on self, God, consciousness, and liberation.
- [Plato's Cave and Maya: Why Advaita Goes Beyond Plato's Allegory](https://www.opensadhaka.com/platos-cave-and-maya): Plato's cave and Maya compared through Republic Book VII, Shankara's adhyasa doctrine, and Advaita's claim that illusion is not only epistemic but ontological.
- [Nietzsche and Vedanta: What His Critique Hits and What It Misses](https://www.opensadhaka.com/nietzsche-and-vedanta): Nietzsche and Vedanta compared through ressentiment, ascetic ideals, Advaita, Tantra, and Kashmir Shaivism, with clear distinctions on selfhood, life affirmation, and liberation.
- [Existentialism and Vedanta: Freedom Begins in Different Places](https://www.opensadhaka.com/existentialism-and-vedanta): Existentialism and Vedanta compared through Sartre, anxiety, freedom, essence, and self inquiry, showing why they diagnose human identity from radically different starting points.
- [Carl Jung and Vedanta: Depth Psychology Is Not the Absolute](https://www.opensadhaka.com/carl-jung-and-vedanta): Carl Jung and Vedanta compared through individuation, archetypes, Zimmer, shadow work, and Advaita's critique that the Absolute cannot be reduced to psychic structure.
- [Neuroscience of Meditation and Hindu Practice: What Evidence Supports](https://www.opensadhaka.com/neuroscience-of-meditation-hinduism): Neuroscience of meditation through a Hindu lens: what brain research confirms, what it cannot measure, and how japa, dhyana, and bhakti differ.
- [Hard Problem of Consciousness and Vedanta: The Question Changes If Matter Is Not Primary](https://www.opensadhaka.com/consciousness-hard-problem-vedanta): The hard problem of consciousness through David Chalmers and Advaita Vedanta, showing why the puzzle looks different once consciousness is treated as primary rather than produced by matter.
- [Hindu Goddess Explained: Devi, Shakti, and the Feminine Divine](https://www.opensadhaka.com/hindu-goddess-explained): Hindu goddess explained for beginners: who is Devi, what Shakti means, and how Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kali, and Parvati relate.
- [Ramayana Explained: Story, Characters, and Why It Still Matters](https://www.opensadhaka.com/ramayana-explained): Ramayana explained for modern readers: key story arc, Rama-Sita-Hanuman-Ravana dynamics, ethical dilemmas, and enduring relevance.
- [How to Read the Upanishads as a Western Beginner](https://www.opensadhaka.com/how-to-read-upanishads-western-beginner): How to read the Upanishads without overwhelm: best entry texts, translation choices, reading sequence, and practical integration tips.
- [Vedas vs Upanishads Explained: What's the Difference?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/vedas-vs-upanishads-explained): Vedas vs Upanishads explained simply: structure, purpose, ritual vs realization, and why Upanishads are called the philosophical culmination.
- [Bhagavad Gita vs Bible: A Respectful Comparative Guide](https://www.opensadhaka.com/bhagavad-gita-vs-bible): Bhagavad Gita vs Bible compared respectfully: genre, theology, ethics, salvation/liberation, and how readers can study both deeply.
- [Vedanta vs Buddhism: Self, Emptiness, and Liberation Compared](https://www.opensadhaka.com/vedanta-vs-buddhism): Vedanta vs Buddhism explained through the Atman and Anatman dispute, Shankara's critique of Buddhist schools, points of convergence, and why their liberation frameworks are not interchangeable.

- [The True Meaning of Sanatan Dharma (And How It Differs from Hinduism)](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-sanatan-dharma): Sanatan Dharma means 'the eternal order' — a universal philosophy of dharma, karma, and moksha predating the geographical label 'Hinduism.' Learn what it actually means and how to live it.

- [What is Maya in Indian Philosophy? Illusion, Mithya, and Moksha](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-maya): Maya doesn't mean the world is fake. It means the world has conditional reality, not absolute reality. A precise guide to maya, mithya, and how moksha is achieved in Advaita Vedanta.
- [The Spiritual Meaning of a Midlife Crisis (And How to Actually Fix It)](https://www.opensadhaka.com/midlife-crisis-spiritual-meaning): A midlife crisis is not a psychological defect — it is a natural spiritual transition. - [Overcoming the Fear of Death Through Advaita Vedanta](https://www.opensadhaka.com/fear-of-death-advaita-vedanta): The fear of death in Eastern philosophy stems from a case of mistaken identity. Advaita Vedanta teaches that you are not the body — and what is not born cannot die.

Spiritual bypassing is using spiritual concepts to avoid genuine suffering. Learn to tell them apart.

## Concept explorer — Sanskrit vocabulary in depth

Definition pages for core Sanskrit concepts. Each page answers "What is X?" with a short definition, philosophical role, practical application, and linked source texts.

- [What is Action / Deed / Cause and Effect?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-karma): The universal principle of cause and effect, action and reaction, which governs all consciousness.
- [What is Righteousness / Duty / Cosmic Order?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-dharma): The underlying order in nature and human life and behavior considered to be in accord with that order.
- [What is Liberation / Emancipation?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-moksha): Freedom from the cycle of birth and death (samsara) and the realization of one's true nature.
- [What is The Cycle of Rebirth / Worldly Existence?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-samsara): The continuous cycle of birth, life, death, and reincarnation.
- [What is Illusion / Measurable Power?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-maya): The cosmic illusion that conceals the true nature of reality and projects the apparent multiplicity of the world.
- [What is Self / Soul / Spirit?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-atman): The innermost, eternal core of a person; the true self.
- [What is The Absolute / Supreme Reality?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-brahman): The transcendent and immanent ultimate reality, supreme cosmic spirit.
- [What is Union / Yoke / Discipline?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-yoga): Physical, mental, and spiritual practices or disciplines which originated in ancient India.
- [What is Non-violence / Harmlessness?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-ahimsa): The ethical principle of not causing harm to other living beings.
- [What is Teacher / Remover of Darkness?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-guru): A personal spiritual teacher or guide who leads the student from ignorance to enlightenment.
- [What is Devotion / Loving Participation in the Divine?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-bhakti): The path of loving devotion, surrender, and heartfelt relationship with the Divine.
- [What is Spiritual Knowledge / Wisdom?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-jnana): Direct spiritual knowledge that reveals the difference between the real and the unreal.
- [What is Discernment / Discrimination?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-viveka): The faculty of discerning the eternal from the transient and the real from the unreal.
- [What is Dispassion / Non-Attachment?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-vairagya): Freedom from compulsive attachment to pleasure, possession, and identity in the transient world.
- [What is Absorption / Perfect Integration?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-samadhi): A state of profound meditative absorption in which the ordinary sense of separateness falls away.
- [What is Selfless Service?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-seva): Action performed in a spirit of service without egoic expectation of reward or recognition.
- [What is Ignorance / Misapprehension?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-avidya): Fundamental spiritual ignorance that obscures true reality and causes mistaken identity.
- [What is Lord / Personal God / Supreme Ruler?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-ishvara): The personal dimension of the Divine understood as Lord, ruler, or supreme guiding intelligence.
- [What is Individual Soul / Living Being?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-jiva): The individual embodied being that experiences life through mind, body, karma, and rebirth.
- [What is The Yoga of Selfless Action?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-karma-yoga): A path of spiritual growth through action performed without attachment to personal reward.
- [What is The Royal Path of Meditation?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-raja-yoga): The disciplined path of mastering mind and consciousness through meditative and psychological training.
- [What is Aims of Human Life?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-purushartha): The four classical aims of human life: Dharma, Artha, Kama, and Moksha.
- [What is Non-Duality / Not-Two?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-advaita): The philosophical view that ultimate reality is one without a second and that separation is only apparent.
- [What is Ego-Maker / Sense of I?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-ahamkara): The principle that constructs the egoic sense of individuality and identification.
- [What is Desireless Action / Action Without Attachment?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-niskama-karma): Acting fully and responsibly without attachment to personal gain or the fruits of action.
- [What is Breath Regulation / Expansion of Vital Energy?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-pranayama): The yogic discipline of regulating breath to steady mind, energy, and awareness.
- [What is Cosmic Order / Sacred Rhythm?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-rta): The primordial cosmic order that sustains truth, harmony, and right relation in the universe.
- [What is Sacred Sound / Instrument of the Mind?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-mantra): A sacred sound, phrase, or syllable used to focus the mind, refine consciousness, and invoke a specific spiritual force or divine presence.
- [What is Repetition of Sacred Sound?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-japa): The repeated chanting or inward repetition of a mantra as a focused spiritual practice.
- [What is Meditation / Sustained Contemplation?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-dhyana): A state of continuous meditative flow in which attention rests steadily on its object without frequent interruption.
- [What is Spiritual Practice / Disciplined Path?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-sadhana): The intentional, repeated spiritual discipline through which a seeker turns aspiration into lived transformation.
- [What is Primordial Sound / Sacred Syllable?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-om): The primordial sacred syllable that symbolizes total reality and serves as a sonic gateway to meditation and divine remembrance.
- [What is Qualities of Nature / Constituent Forces?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-guna): The three foundational qualities of material nature—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—that shape mind, behavior, and experience.
- [What is Divine Descent / Incarnation?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-avatara): A manifestation of the Divine that descends into the world to restore order, protect Dharma, and guide beings toward truth.
- [What is Austerity / Spiritual Heat / Discipline?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-tapas): The purifying heat generated by disciplined effort, restraint, and voluntary acceptance of constructive difficulty.
- [What is Concentration / Mental Holding?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-dharana): The disciplined act of holding the mind steadily on one chosen object, point, or field of attention.
- [What is Divine Play / Cosmic Playfulness?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-lila): The vision of creation and divine activity as a spontaneous play of consciousness rather than a mechanical act of necessity.
- [What is Truthfulness / Reality?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-satya): The practice of absolute honesty and aligning oneself with what is real rather than what is comfortable.
- [What is Vital Life Force / Breath?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-prana): The animating energy that drives all physical, mental, and cosmic activity, most visibly tracked through the breath.
- [What is Energy Center / Wheel?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-chakra): A concentrated hub of subtle energy (Prana) in the body where specific psychological drives, emotions, and physical functions intersect.
- [What is Direct Wisdom / Insight?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-prajna): Spontaneous, direct knowledge that arises without the need for intellectual reasoning or conceptual thought.
- [What is Peace / Tranquility?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-shanti): A profound state of inner peace that remains undisturbed regardless of external circumstances.
- [What is Coiled Power / Latent Energy?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-kundalini): The dormant, evolutionary cosmic energy residing at the base of the spine, which when awakened, drives spiritual transformation.
- [What is Channel / Stream?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-nadi): The subtle energetic pathways through which Prana flows in the human body.
- [What is Sheath / Layer?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-kosha): The five concentric layers of experience that cover the true Self (Atman), from dense matter to pure bliss.
- [What is Seal / Gesture?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-mudra): Specific physical gestures—often of the hands—used to direct subtle energy, lock in focus, and induce specific states of mind.
- [What is Lock / Bond?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-bandha): Internal muscular and energetic locks used to capture, compress, and direct the flow of Prana within the body.
- [What is Seat / Posture?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-asana): The steady, comfortable physical posture required to minimize bodily distraction during deep meditation.
- [What is Vitality / Immunity?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-ojas): The refined subtle essence of physical digestion and vitality that provides immunity, stability, and enduring strength.
- [What is Radiance / Fire?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-tejas): The subtle essence of digestion, intelligence, and transformation that manifests as charisma, mental clarity, and spiritual fire.
- [What is Point / Seed?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-bindu): The infinitely small, dimensionless point of concentrated energy and consciousness from which the universe expands.
- [What is Ritual Worship / Adoration?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-puja): A highly structured ritual offering of reverence, honoring a divine guest through physical actions, mantras, and sensory gifts.
- [What is Sacrifice / Sacred Fire Offering?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-yajna): The ancient Vedic ritual of fire offering, symbolizing the broader spiritual principle that life itself is a continuous offering to the cosmic fire.
- [What is Chanting / Devotional Song?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-kirtan): The communal, ecstatic singing of mantras and divine names, designed to temporarily bypass the intellect and flood the emotional system with devotion.
- [What is Instrument / Mystical Diagram?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-yantra): A precise geometric diagram used as a highly focused tool or 'machine' for meditation, concentration, and visualizing cosmic forces.
- [What is Resolve / Intention?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-sankalpa): A deeply held, one-pointed resolve or vow set at the beginning of a spiritual practice or undertaking to align the subconscious will.
- [What is Auspicious Sight / Vision?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-darshan): The act of beholding the Divine—either through a physical deity or a living saint—and receiving a transmission of grace through that mutual gaze.
- [What is Grace / Blessed Offering?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-prasad): The tangible, material blessing—often in the form of food—returned to a devotee after being offered and consecrated by the Divine.
- [What is Ritual Illuminating / Waving of Light?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-arati): The culminating devotional act of waving a flame before a deity to physically illuminate the Divine and to burn away the worshiper's own ignorance.
- [What is Supreme Consciousness / The Witness?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-purusha): The eternal, unchanging, pure, and passive consciousness that acts solely as the silent witness to reality.
- [What is Primal Nature / Matter?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-prakriti): The massive, dynamic, unconscious matrix of all material and psychological reality, driven entirely by three fundamental forces (Gunas).
- [What is Higher Intellect / Discernment?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-buddhi): The sharpest, most refined faculty of the human mind, responsible for deep discernment, existential decision-making, and wisdom.
- [What is Sensory Mind / The Doubter?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-manas): The lower, processing layer of the mind that continuously receives sensory data, remembers the past, worries about the future, and oscillates in doubt.
- [What is Mind-Stuff / Subconscious Storehouse?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-chitta): The vast, largely submerged subconscious repository of all memories, latent impressions, fears, and conditioning.
- [What is Fluctuation / Thought-Wave?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-vritti): Any active thought, memory, perception, or emotion rippling across the surface of the mind.
- [What is Affliction / Psychological Knot?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-klesha): The five innate psychological conditionings that generate all human suffering, rooted in fundamental ignorance.
- [What is Impression / Subconscious Groove?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/what-is-samskara): The subtle psychological scar or groove left on the mind by every action, which predisposes an individual to repeat that same action.

## Deities

Profile pages for principal deities — iconography, mythology, philosophical meaning, and associated mantras and stotras.

- [Shiva](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/shiva): Who is Shiva? Shiva is the transforming principle in Hindu thought: yogi, destroyer of ignorance, and source of inner stillness and liberation.
- [Vishnu](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/vishnu): Who is Vishnu? Vishnu is the sustaining principle of cosmic order, preserving dharma through compassion, intelligence, and avataric descent.
- [Brahma](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/brahma): Who is Brahma? Brahma is the creator aspect in the Trimurti, symbolizing emergence, knowledge, and cosmic structure.
- [Krishna](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/krishna): Who is Krishna? Krishna is a central deity in Hinduism, revered as Vishnu's avatar, teacher of the Bhagavad Gita, and embodiment of divine love.
- [Rama](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/rama): Who is Rama? Rama is Vishnu's avatar of dharmic kingship, moral clarity, and disciplined compassion.
- [Hanuman](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/hanuman): Who is Hanuman? Hanuman is the exemplar of devotion, courage, and disciplined strength, revered for unwavering service to Rama and dharma.
- [Ganesha](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/ganesha): Who is Ganesha? Ganesha is the remover of obstacles and lord of beginnings, symbolizing discernment, grounded intelligence, and auspicious action.
- [Lakshmi](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/lakshmi): Who is Lakshmi? Lakshmi is the goddess of auspicious abundance, beauty, and ethical prosperity aligned with dharma and inner harmony.
- [Saraswati](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/saraswati): Who is Saraswati? Saraswati is the goddess of wisdom, language, music, and refined intelligence.
- [Durga](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/durga): Who is Durga? Durga is the protective warrior goddess who overcomes chaos and restores sacred order.
- [Kali](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/kali): Who is Kali? Kali is the fierce compassionate force of radical transformation and ego-cutting grace.
- [Parvati](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/parvati): Who is Parvati? Parvati is the goddess of devotion, strength, and sacred relationship, consort of Shiva.
- [Kartikeya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/kartikeya): Who is Kartikeya? Kartikeya is the warrior-son of Shiva and Parvati, associated with courage, strategy, and youthful power.
- [Radha](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/radha): Who is Radha? Radha is the supreme devotional counterpart of Krishna, symbolizing pure love and total surrender.
- [Sita](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/sita): Who is Sita? Sita is the Ramayana's embodiment of dignity, devotion, endurance, and moral strength.
- [Indra](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/indra): Who is Indra? Indra is the Vedic king of devas, associated with storm power, leadership, and cosmic battle.
- [Surya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/surya): Who is Surya? Surya is the solar deity of vitality, illumination, health, and disciplined rhythm.
- [Chandra](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/chandra): Who is Chandra? Chandra is the lunar deity associated with mind, emotion, rhythm, and reflective awareness.
- [Agni](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/agni): Who is Agni? Agni is the sacred fire deity, mediator of offerings, transformation, and spiritual energy.
- [Yama](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/yama): Who is Yama? Yama is the deity of ethical order, mortality, and post-death justice.
- [Narasimha](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/narasimha): Who is Narasimha? Narasimha is Vishnu's fierce protective avatar, symbolizing divine intervention when justice must be restored immediately.
- [Dattatreya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/dattatreya): Who is Dattatreya? Dattatreya is the avadhuta sage-deity of integrated wisdom, often seen as a synthesis of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva principles.
- [Ayyappa](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/ayyappa): Who is Ayyappa? Ayyappa is a major South Indian deity associated with disciplined pilgrimage, vow-based practice, and protective devotion.
- [Kubera](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/kubera): Who is Kubera? Kubera is the guardian of wealth and stewardship, associated with ethical prosperity and responsible resource holding.
- [Varuna](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/varuna): Who is Varuna? Varuna is the Vedic deity of cosmic order, waters, and moral law.
- [Vayu](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/vayu): Who is Vayu? Vayu is the deity of wind, movement, and life-force flow, linked to breath and vitality.
- [Bhairava](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/bhairava): Who is Bhairava? Bhairava is a fierce Shaiva form representing uncompromising awareness, protection, and ego-dissolving intensity.
- [Ardhanarishvara](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/ardhanarishvara): Who is Ardhanarishvara? Ardhanarishvara is the integrated form of Shiva and Shakti, symbolizing inseparability of consciousness and energy.
- [Tara](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/tara): Who is Tara? Tara is the second Mahavidya, the goddess of guidance across crisis, speech-power, and protective wisdom in the Shakta Tantric tradition.
- [Tripura Sundari](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/tripura-sundari): Who is Tripura Sundari? Tripura Sundari is the third Mahavidya, the goddess of beauty across three worlds, sovereign of the Sri Yantra, and heart of the Shri Vidya tradition.
- [Bhuvaneshvari](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/bhuvaneshvari): Who is Bhuvaneshvari? Bhuvaneshvari is the fourth Mahavidya, the goddess of space itself, sovereign of all worlds, and the Shakta understanding of cosmic expansion.
- [Bhairavi](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/bhairavi): Who is Bhairavi? Bhairavi is the fifth Mahavidya, the fierce goddess of tapas, the burning away of impurities, and the heat that precedes realization.
- [Chhinnamasta](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/chhinnamasta): Who is Chhinnamasta? Chhinnamasta is the sixth Mahavidya, the self-decapitated goddess who severs her own head to feed her attendants, representing radical self-sacrifice and the circuit of life-force.
- [Dhumavati](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/dhumavati): Who is Dhumavati? Dhumavati is the seventh Mahavidya, the widow goddess of smoke, disappointment, and the void left when all comfort is removed.
- [Bagalamukhi](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/bagalamukhi): Who is Bagalamukhi? Bagalamukhi is the eighth Mahavidya, the goddess of stambhana (paralysis), who freezes enemies, delusion, and the compulsive movement of mind.
- [Matangi](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/matangi): Who is Matangi? Matangi is the ninth Mahavidya, the outcaste goddess of speech, art, and the sacred within the polluted, transgressing purity-pollution boundaries.
- [Kamalatmika](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/kamalatmika): Who is Kamalatmika? Kamalatmika is the tenth Mahavidya, the Tantric Lakshmi, representing the fullness of manifest reality, material and spiritual abundance, and the completion of the Mahavidya cycle.
- [Kala Bhairava](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/kala-bhairava): Who is Kala Bhairava? Kala Bhairava is the lord of time and the fiercest form of Bhairava, guardian of Kashi and destroyer of the fear of death.
- [Batuk Bhairava](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/batuk-bhairava): Who is Batuk Bhairava? Batuk Bhairava is the child form of Bhairava, associated with protection, removal of obstacles, and initiation into Shaiva practice.
- [Tripura Bhairavi](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/tripura-bhairavi): Who is Tripura Bhairavi? Tripura Bhairavi is the fierce aspect of Tripura Sundari, the burning force of tapas that purifies the three worlds.
- [Mangala](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/mangala): Who is Mangala? Mangala is the graha of disciplined courage, vitality, initiative, and constructive use of force in Jyotish.
- [Budha](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/budha): Who is Budha? Budha is the graha of intellect, speech, learning, analysis, and adaptable intelligence in Jyotish.
- [Brihaspati](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/brihaspati): Who is Brihaspati? Brihaspati is the guru-graha of wisdom, counsel, ethics, learning, and expansive insight.
- [Shukra](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/shukra): Who is Shukra? Shukra is the graha of beauty, relationship, enjoyment, refinement, and value alignment in Jyotish.
- [Shani](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/shani): Who is Shani? Shani is the graha of time, discipline, karma, endurance, humility, and maturing responsibility.
- [Rahu](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/rahu): Who is Rahu? Rahu is the north node archetype of hunger, disruption, foreignness, obsession, amplification, and unconventional growth.
- [Ketu](https://www.opensadhaka.com/deities/ketu): Who is Ketu? Ketu is the south node archetype of detachment, moksha impulse, severance, mystical insight, and inwardization.

## Mantras

Canonical mantras with etymology, usage, and context. Each page gives the one-line meaning, word-by-word breakdown, and practice notes (best time, repetitions, tradition).

- [Om Namah Shivaya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-namah-shivaya): I bow to Shiva, the auspicious inner consciousness.
- [Gayatri Mantra](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/gayatri-mantra): May the divine light illumine our intellect.
- [Maha Mrityunjaya Mantra](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/mahamrityunjaya-mantra): May we be liberated from fear and mortality, like a ripe fruit released from its stem.
- [Om Namo Narayanaya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-namo-narayanaya): I bow to Narayana, the sustaining divine presence.
- [Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-namo-bhagavate-vasudevaya): I bow to Bhagavan Vasudeva, the indwelling Lord.
- [Soham](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/soham): I am That.
- [Om Shanti](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-shanti): Invocation of peace at personal, relational, and cosmic levels.
- [Hanuman Chalisa](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/hanuman-chalisa): Forty-verse devotional hymn invoking Hanuman's courage and protection.
- [Ram Ram Ram](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/ram-ram-ram): Repetition of Rama-nama for purification and devotional steadiness.
- [Hari Om](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/hari-om): Invocation of the divine as remover and harmonizer of suffering.
- [Om Gam Ganapataye Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-gam-ganapataye-namah): I bow to Ganesha, remover of obstacles and lord of wise beginnings.
- [Om Shreem Mahalakshmyai Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-shreem-mahalakshmyai-namah): I bow to Mahalakshmi, source of auspicious abundance and harmony.
- [Om Aim Saraswatyai Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-aim-saraswatyai-namah): I bow to Saraswati, goddess of wisdom, speech, and learning.
- [Om Dum Durgayei Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-dum-durgayei-namah): I bow to Durga, protective force who removes fear and adversity.
- [Krim Kalikayai Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/krim-kalikayai-namah): I bow to Kali, transformative power that dissolves fear and false identity.
- [Om Hanumate Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-hanumate-namah): I bow to Hanuman, embodiment of courage, devotion, and service.
- [Swamiye Sharanam Ayyappa](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/swamiye-sharanam-ayyappa): I take refuge in Lord Ayyappa.
- [Kaal Bhairav Ashtakam](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/kaal-bhairav-ashtakam): A devotional hymn invoking Bhairava's protective and time-transcending grace.
- [Shantakaram Bhujagashayanam](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/shantakaram-bhujagashayanam): A Vishnu dhyana verse invoking serenity, protection, and cosmic steadiness.
- [Nirvana Shatakam (Mano Buddhyahankara)](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/nirvana-shatakam): A non-dual contemplative chant declaring identity beyond body-mind and ego.
- [Lokah Samastah Sukhino Bhavantu](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/lokah-samastah-sukhino-bhavantu): May all beings everywhere be happy and free.
- [Asato Ma Sadgamaya (Pavamana Mantra)](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/asato-ma-sadgamaya): Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality.
- [Tvameva Mata](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/tvameva-mata): You alone are my mother, father, friend, knowledge, wealth -- everything.
- [Om Hram Hrim Hraum Sah Suryaya Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-hram-hrim-hraum-sah-suryaya-namah): I bow to Surya, source of clarity, vitality, and illumining discipline.
- [Om Shram Shrim Shraum Sah Chandraya Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-shram-shrim-shraum-sah-chandraya-namah): I bow to Chandra, cooling mind and emotional rhythm.
- [Om Kram Krim Kraum Sah Bhaumaya Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-kram-krim-kraum-sah-bhaumaya-namah): I bow to Mangala, source of disciplined courage and directed energy.
- [Om Bram Brim Braum Sah Budhaya Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-bram-brim-braum-sah-budhaya-namah): I bow to Budha, source of speech, learning, and discrimination.
- [Om Gram Grim Graum Sah Gurave Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-gram-grim-graum-sah-gurave-namah): I bow to Brihaspati, the guru principle of wisdom and counsel.
- [Om Dram Drim Draum Sah Shukraya Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-dram-drim-draum-sah-shukraya-namah): I bow to Shukra, source of refinement, harmony, and balanced enjoyment.
- [Om Pram Prim Praum Sah Shanaishcharaya Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-pram-prim-praum-sah-shanaishcharaya-namah): I bow to Shani, teacher of time, discipline, humility, and karmic responsibility.
- [Om Bhram Bhrim Bhraum Sah Rahave Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-bhram-bhrim-bhraum-sah-rahave-namah): I bow to Rahu, asking for discernment amidst obsession, disruption, and intensity.
- [Om Sram Srim Sraum Sah Ketave Namah](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/om-sram-srim-sraum-sah-ketave-namah): I bow to Ketu, the force of detachment, simplification, and inward insight.
- [Navagraha Stotram](https://www.opensadhaka.com/mantras/navagraha-stotram): A nine-verse hymn honoring the Navagraha as archetypal forces of rhythm, karma, and spiritual reflection.

## Stotras and Sahasranamas

Verse-by-verse and name-by-name treatments of devotional texts, each with Devanagari, transliteration, word-by-word translation, and literary/philosophical analysis.

- [Lalita Sahasranama](https://www.opensadhaka.com/stotras/lalita-sahasranama) (1000 names): The 1000 names of the Divine Mother Lalita from the Brahmanda Purana, revealed by Hayagriva to the sage Agastya.
- [Navagraha Stotram](https://www.opensadhaka.com/stotras/navagraha-stotram) (9 verses): A nine-verse hymn honoring the nine grahas as sacred archetypal forces of rhythm, karma, and contemplative alignment.
- [Shiva Tandava Stotram](https://www.opensadhaka.com/stotras/shiva-tandava-stotram) (16 verses): Composed by Ravana in reverence to Lord Shiva — 16 verses describing Shiva's cosmic Tandava dance with extraordinary poetic power.
- [Vishnu Sahasranama](https://www.opensadhaka.com/stotras/vishnu-sahasranama) (107 verses): The 1000 names of Lord Vishnu from the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata, recited by Bhishma to Yudhishthira as the supreme means of liberation. Composed in 107 shlokas in Anushtup meter.

## Comparisons (X vs Y)

Direct philosophical and practical comparisons between schools, concepts, teachers, and practices. Each page opens with a TL;DR that distills the central distinction.

- [Advaita vs Dvaita Vedanta: Non-Duality vs Dualism](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/advaita-vs-dvaita): Advaita Vedanta teaches that the individual soul (Atman) and the ultimate reality (Brahman) are strictly identical. Dvaita Vedanta teaches that the soul and God are eternally distinct.
- [Advaita vs Vishishtadvaita: Shankara vs Ramanuja](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/advaita-vs-vishishtadvaita): Both agree that Brahman is the supreme reality. But Shankara says souls and the world are ultimately unreal (illusory). Ramanuja says souls and the world are real — they are the 'body' of Brahman, distinct but never separate.
- [Shaivism vs Vaishnavism: Two Paths of Devotion](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/shaivism-vs-vaishnavism): Both are devotional paths within Sanatan Dharma. Shaivism centers on Shiva as the Supreme — the ascetic, the destroyer, the yogi's yogi. Vaishnavism centers on Vishnu (and his avatars Krishna, Rama) — the preserver, the lover, the social ideal.
- [Samkhya vs Yoga Philosophy: Theory vs Practice](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/samkhya-vs-yoga): Samkhya is the map; Yoga is the journey. Samkhya explains the structure of reality (25 principles, two eternal substances). Yoga gives the method — eight practical limbs — to experience that truth directly.
- [Japa vs Dhyana: Mantra Repetition vs Silent Meditation](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/japa-vs-dhyana): Japa gives the restless mind a sacred anchor — a mantra to hold onto. Dhyana asks you to release even that anchor and rest in pure awareness. Both lead to the same silence, through different doors.
- [Vipassana vs Transcendental Meditation](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/vipassana-vs-transcendental-meditation): Vipassana asks you to observe the raw, unfiltered reality of mind and body without flinching — discomfort is the curriculum. TM gives the mind a mantra-vehicle and lets it dive inward into effortless stillness. Two very different entry points to the same silent depth.
- [Hatha Yoga vs Raja Yoga](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/hatha-yoga-vs-raja-yoga): Hatha Yoga prepares the physical body and its energy systems for deep meditation. Raja Yoga is that deep meditation — the direct science of controlling the mind. Hatha is the preparation; Raja is the destination. Most modern 'yoga' is Hatha; most classical yoga philosophy is Raja.
- [Bhakti Yoga vs Jnana Yoga: Devotion vs Knowledge](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/bhakti-vs-jnana): Bhakti Yoga dissolves the ego through love — surrendering completely to a personal God. Jnana Yoga dissolves the ego through inquiry — investigating the nature of the 'I' until it evaporates. Both paths lead to Moksha; your temperament determines which vehicle fits you.
- [Mindfulness vs Dhyana: Western vs Vedic Meditation](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/mindfulness-vs-dhyana): Mindfulness, as practiced in the West, is primarily used for stress reduction and present-moment awareness. Dhyana (Vedic meditation) is a profound state of concentration intended to lead beyond the mind entirely.
- [Stoicism vs Vedanta: East Meets West](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/stoicism-vs-vedanta): Both Stoicism and Vedanta teach that peace comes from mastering your inner world, not controlling external events. Stoicism focuses on virtue and rational self-discipline within the flow of Nature. Vedanta goes further — it questions whether the 'self' doing the controlling is real at all.
- [Western Psychology vs Yoga Philosophy](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/psychology-vs-yoga-philosophy): Western psychology studies and heals the mind from within the framework of the mind itself. Yoga philosophy maps the entire territory of consciousness — from ego to pure awareness — and offers a direct route to the level of consciousness where all psychological problems become irrelevant.
- [Freud's Unconscious vs Patanjali's Chitta](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/freud-vs-patanjali): Freud's unconscious holds repressed drives, memories, and conflicts that leak into behavior through symptoms and dreams. Patanjali's Chitta holds Samskaras — deep impressions from all past experience — that shape every perception and reaction. Both systems agree the invisible past drives the present. Their solutions differ radically.
- [Sin vs Karma: Western Guilt vs Eastern Consequence](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sin-vs-karma): Sin is a moral transgression against God requiring forgiveness. Karma is a natural law of cause and effect — morally neutral, like gravity. Sin implies guilt; Karma implies consequence. The difference changes everything about how you relate to suffering and responsibility.
- [Karma vs Dharma: What's the Difference?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/karma-vs-dharma): Karma is the law of cause and effect — every action you take creates a future experience. Dharma is your duty, your nature, the right path for you. Karma describes what happens; Dharma describes what should happen.
- [Maya vs Illusion: Is the World Real?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/maya-vs-illusion): An illusion is a misperception of something that doesn't exist. Maya is something more subtle: it is the misperception of something that does exist, but whose true nature is hidden. The world is real — but what you think it is, is not.
- [Atman vs Brahman: Self and Absolute](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/atman-vs-brahman): Brahman is the infinite, universal consciousness — the ground of all being. Atman is the individual soul — what you really are beneath the body, mind, and personality. Advaita's revolutionary claim: Atman and Brahman are ultimately identical. The drop and the ocean are the same water.
- [Moksha vs Mukti: Are They the Same?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/moksha-vs-mukti): Moksha and Mukti are often used interchangeably, and both mean liberation. But Moksha tends to emphasize the positive fullness of the liberated state, while Mukti means 'release' — freedom from bondage. The difference is like 'arriving home' vs 'leaving prison.' Same destination, different emphasis.
- [Sadhaka vs Sadhguru App: Which is Right for You?](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sadhaka-vs-sadhguru-app): The Sadhguru App delivers one lineage, one teacher, one system. Sadhaka is a discovery platform for the entire ocean of Sanatan Dharma — helping you find the tradition, practice, and philosophy that fits your unique nature.
- [Sadhaka vs Insight Timer](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sadhaka-vs-insight-timer): Insight Timer is a vast marketplace — like a spiritual buffet with 100,000 items. Sadhaka is a structured path with a knowledgeable guide. Both have value; the question is whether you need breadth or depth right now.
- [Sadhaka vs Headspace: Dharma vs McMindfulness](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sadhaka-vs-headspace): Headspace offers a polished, secular, Netflix-style meditation experience optimized for busy professionals. Sadhaka offers the depth of India's living spiritual traditions for those who have outgrown stress-reduction and are seeking genuine transformation.
- [Tantra vs Vedanta: Two Paths to the Same Summit](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/tantra-vs-vedanta): Vedanta seeks liberation by denying the world (Neti, Neti - Not this, Not this). Tantra seeks liberation by embracing the world as the Goddess's own power. One is a path of subtraction, the other a path of expansion.
- [Sanyasa vs Grihastha: Renunciation vs Householder Path](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sanyasa-vs-grihastha): Sanyasa is the total commitment to spiritual life through the abandonment of social roles. Grihastha is the path of spiritual growth within the structures of family, work, and society. Both are valid 'Ashramas' for reaching the highest truth.
- [Karma Yoga vs Jnana Yoga: Action vs Wisdom](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/karma-yoga-vs-jnana-yoga): Karma Yoga purifies the heart through selfless service and action without attachment. Jnana Yoga clears the mind through inquiry and discrimination. They are two wings of the same bird, often practiced together to achieve balance.
- [Raja Yoga vs Kundalini Yoga: Mind vs Energy](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/raja-yoga-vs-kundalini-yoga): Raja Yoga focuses on stilling the mind through meditation and ethics (Patanjali's 8 limbs). Kundalini Yoga focuses on awakening the latent spiritual energy (Shakti) within the body and raising it through the chakras. One is the path of the Witness; the other is the path of the Energy.
- [Shaiva Siddhanta vs Kashmir Shaivism](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/shaiva-siddhanta-vs-kashmir-shaivism): Shaiva Siddhanta (South) is primarily dualistic: God (Pati), souls (Pashu), and the world (Pasha) are all eternally real and distinct. Kashmir Shaivism (North) is strictly non-dual: Everything is Shiva, and there is no real difference between the Lord and the soul.
- [Advaita Vedanta vs Buddhism: Non-Dualism Compared](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/advaita-vs-buddhism): Advaita says there is an eternal, unchanging Self (Atman) that is the Ground of Being. Buddhism says there is no permanent Self (Anatman) and reality is Emptiness (Sunyata). Two paths that sound similar but differ on the very foundation of existence.
- [Vaishnavism vs Shaktism: Vishnu vs the Goddess](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/vaishnavism-vs-shaktism): Vaishnavism centers on Vishnu and his avatars (Krishna, Rama) as the supreme personal God of love and Dharma. Shaktism centers on Devi (Durga, Kali, Lakshmi) as the primordial power that creates, sustains, and destroys the universe. One is the path of the Lord; the other is the path of the Mother.
- [Navavidha Bhakti vs Ashtanga Yoga: Love vs Discipline](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/navavidha-bhakti-vs-ashtanga-yoga): Navavidha Bhakti is the path of the Heart, using nine relational practices (singing, remembering, serving) to find God. Ashtanga Yoga is the path of the Mind and Body, using eight limbs of discipline (postures, breath, meditation) to find Stillness. Two distinct technologies of transformation.
- [Ramana Maharshi vs Nisargadatta Maharaj](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/ramana-maharshi-vs-nisargadatta-maharaj): Ramana Maharshi taught the direct method of 'Who Am I?' through silence and steady inquiry. Nisargadatta Maharaj taught the path of 'Abiding in the I Am' through sharp, intellectual pointers and fiery discourse. Both represent the pinnacle of Advaita Bhakti.
- [Adi Shankaracharya vs Ramanuja: Two Pillars of Vedanta](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/adi-shankaracharya-vs-ramanuja): Shankara taught that the world is an illusion (Maya) and the soul is identical to Brahman. Ramanuja taught that the world is real and the soul is an eternal, distinct part of Brahman. It's the classic debate between Pure Knowledge and Divine Love.
- [Swami Vivekananda vs Sri Ramakrishna: Master and Disciple](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/swami-vivekananda-vs-ramakrishna): Ramakrishna was the embodiment of direct mystical experience, seeing no difference between religions. Vivekananda was the 'Man-maker' who rationalized and organized these experiences into a global mission of service and strength.
- [Sadhguru vs Osho: Neo-Vedanta Compared](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sadhguru-vs-osho): Sadhguru emphasizes 'Inner Engineering'—a systematic, technology-based approach to well-being and yoga. Osho emphasized 'Rebellion'—stripping away social conditioning and personal ego through celebration, meditation, and radical honesty.
- [Paramahansa Yogananda vs Maharishi Mahesh Yogi](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/paramahansa-yogananda-vs-maharishi-mahesh-yogi): Yogananda emphasized Kriya Yoga—a comprehensive path of devotion, energy control, and Christ-consciousness. Maharishi emphasized Transcendental Meditation (TM)—an effortless technique for mental rest and cosmic consciousness.
- [J. Krishnamurti vs Chögyam Trungpa](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/krishnamurti-vs-chogyam-trungpa): Krishnamurti was an ascetic intellectual who told seekers to 'be a light unto yourself' and reject all gurus. Trungpa was a Vajrayana master who used alcohol, relationship, and shock ('Crazy Wisdom') to break seekers out of their 'spiritual materialism'.
- [Nagarjuna vs Adi Shankara: Emptiness vs Non-Duality](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/nagarjuna-vs-adi-shankara): Nagarjuna used logic to show that all things are 'Empty' of inherent existence (Sunyata). Shankara used logic to show that all things are 'One' in their ultimate reality (Brahman). To an untrained ear, they sound the same; to the seeker, they are two different voids.
- [Sri Ramakrishna vs Chaitanya Mahaprabhu](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/ramakrishna-vs-chaitanya-mahaprabhu): Chaitanya (15th Century) was the father of the Kirtan movement, lost in the love of Krishna. Ramakrishna (19th Century) was a universalist mystic who saw the Divine in all paths and deities. Both lived in a state of constant spiritual intoxication.
- [Bhagavad Gita vs Upanishads](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/bhagavad-gita-vs-upanishads): The Upanishads are the philosophical seeds (Shruti); the Bhagavad Gita is the practical fruit (Smriti). The Gita takes the abstract non-duality of the Upanishads and makes it actionable for a person living in the world.
- [Yoga Sutras vs Bhagavad Gita](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/yoga-sutras-vs-bhagavad-gita): The Yoga Sutras are a scientific manual for the mind, focusing on meditation and internal discipline. The Bhagavad Gita is a poetic guide for the heart and life, focusing on relationship and action. Both lead to Yoga (Union), but through different temperaments.
- [Rigveda vs Atharvaveda: Chants vs Spells](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/rigveda-vs-atharvaveda): The Rigveda is the foundation of Vedic philosophy, filled with grand hymns to Cosmic Powers (Devas). The Atharvaveda is the 'Veda of the common man,' filled with prayers for healing, prosperity, and protection in daily life. Transcendent vs Immanent.
- [Mahabharata vs Ramayana: The Epic of Gray vs the Epic of Gold](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/mahabharata-vs-ramayana): The Ramayana is a story of 'Ideal Dharma'—the perfect King, the perfect wife, the perfect brother. The Mahabharata is a story of 'Crisis Dharma'—a world where every choice is difficult, good people make mistakes, and the line between right and wrong is thin.
- [Brahma Sutras vs Upanishads: Logic vs Poetry](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/brahma-sutras-vs-upanishads): The Upanishads are the inspired 'Songs' of the forest sages. The Brahma Sutras are the 'Logic' of the philosophers, organizing and defending those songs against critics. Revelation vs. Systematization.
- [Ashtavakra Gita vs Bhagavad Gita](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/ashtavakra-gita-vs-bhagavad-gita): The Bhagavad Gita is the 'Kindergarten' of Advaita (for everyone); the Ashtavakra Gita is the 'Post-Doctorate' (for those ready for absolute non-duality). The Gita teaches how to act; Ashtavakra teaches how to simply be.
- [Shiva Sutras vs Yoga Sutras](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/shiva-sutras-vs-yoga-sutras): Yoga Sutras focus on 'Nirodha' (Stilling the mind) to separate the soul from matter. Shiva Sutras focus on 'Samatva' (Union) to realize that even the mind and matter are Shiva's own light. Separation vs. Recognition.
- [Narada Bhakti Sutras vs Yoga Sutras](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/narada-bhakti-sutras-vs-yoga-sutras): Narada Bhakti Sutras define Yoga as 'Supreme Love for God.' Patanjali's Yoga Sutras define Yoga as 'Stilling the movements of the mind.' One is a manual for the enthusiast; the other for the engineer.
- [Mantra vs Affirmation: Sacred Sound vs Positive Self-Talk](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/mantra-vs-affirmation): A mantra is a sacred sound-form tied to a deity, tradition, and specific practice rules. An affirmation is a self-directed positive statement. They share repetition as a method but differ in origin, authority, and the theory of how they work.
- [Japa vs Meditation: Mantra Repetition vs Broader Dhyana](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/japa-vs-meditation): Japa is the repetition of a mantra — it is a specific technique within meditation. Meditation (dhyana) is the broader practice of sustained one-pointed attention. Japa gives the mind an object; dhyana is what happens when the mind stays on that object.
- [Mantra vs Prayer: Invocation vs Petition](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/mantra-vs-prayer): Prayer is petition — the devotee asks the divine for something. Mantra is invocation — the practitioner becomes the sound. Prayer works through personal relationship; mantra works through vibratory precision and repetition.
- [Pranayama vs Breathwork: Vedic Prana Control vs Modern Techniques](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/pranayama-vs-breathwork): Pranayama is a Vedic practice aimed at controlling prana (vital energy) as preparation for meditation. Modern breathwork (Wim Hof, holotropic, etc.) focuses on physiological and emotional effects. Pranayama is embedded in a spiritual framework; breathwork is typically secular.
- [Meditation vs Dhyana: The Western Umbrella vs Patanjali's 7th Limb](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/meditation-vs-dhyana): In the West, 'meditation' covers everything from mindfulness apps to Zen sitting. Dhyana, in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (7th limb), means an unbroken flow of attention toward a single object. Dhyana is narrower and more precise than what most Westerners call meditation.
- [Karma Yoga vs Bhakti Yoga: Action vs Devotion](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/karma-yoga-vs-bhakti-yoga): Karma Yoga purifies the mind through selfless action without attachment to results. Bhakti Yoga achieves the same through intense, surrendered love for the Divine. The Bhagavad Gita teaches that both lead to the same liberation.
- [Vedanta vs Buddhism: The Atman vs The Anatman](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/vedanta-vs-buddhism): Vedanta posits an eternal, unchanging, pure consciousness (Atman) as the ground of reality. Buddhism posits the doctrine of Anatman (no-self), arguing that there is no fixed, permanent essence beneath the changing stream of experience.
- [Sanatan Dharma vs Hinduism: Understanding the Names](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sanatan-dharma-vs-hinduism): Sanatan Dharma is the ancient, indigenous term meaning 'The Eternal Law/Way.' Hinduism is a geographic term originally coined by Persians to describe the people living beyond the Indus River.
- [Upanishads vs Vedas: Rituals vs Philosophy](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/upanishads-vs-vedas): The Vedas are the vast, ancient bodies of knowledge primarily focused on hymns and rituals. The Upanishads are the concluding philosophical portions of the Vedas that focus on self-knowledge and the nature of reality.
- [Guru vs Teacher: The Transmission of Wisdom](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/guru-vs-teacher): A teacher imparts information to the intellect. A Guru transmits consciousness and initiates transformation in the disciple. The Guru functions not merely as an instructor, but as a mirror for the disciple's own divine nature.
- [Mantra vs Prayer: Sound Science vs Devotion](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/mantra-vs-prayer): A prayer operates at the level of meaning and emotion; it is a conversation with the Divine. A mantra operates at the level of sound vibration (spanda); its power lies in precise repetition, regardless of the practitioner's intellectual understanding.
- [Puja vs Meditation: Devotion vs Concentration](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/puja-vs-meditation): Puja is the external, embodied practice of devotion involving all the senses. Meditation is the internal, silent practice of concentration and awareness. Both serve to dissolve the ego and fix the mind on the Divine.
- [Sadhguru vs Ramana Maharshi: The Modern Mystic and the Silent Sage](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sadhguru-vs-ramana-maharshi): Sadhguru approaches spirituality through an active, yogic, energetic framework aiming at complete wellbeing and inner engineering. Ramana Maharshi taught through profound silence and Self-Inquiry (Atma Vichara), aiming directly at enlightenment through the realization of the non-dual Self.
- [Sadhaka vs Insight Timer: Focused Tradition vs Broad Variety](https://www.opensadhaka.com/compare/sadhaka-vs-insight-timer): Insight Timer offers thousands of disconnected meditations from every conceivable background. Sadhaka offers a coherent, structured, and philosophically grounded path rooted entirely in the authentic traditions of Sanatan Dharma.

## Philosophical schools

- [Vedanta](https://www.opensadhaka.com/philosophies/vedanta): The culmination of Vedic wisdom exploring the nature of ultimate reality and the self.
- [Advaita Vedanta](https://www.opensadhaka.com/philosophies/advaita): Non-dual philosophy teaching that individual self and universal consciousness are one.
- [Vishishtadvaita](https://www.opensadhaka.com/philosophies/vishishtadvaita): Qualified non-dualism seeing God, souls, and world as distinct yet inseparable.
- [Dvaita](https://www.opensadhaka.com/philosophies/dvaita): Dualist philosophy emphasizing eternal distinction between God, souls, and matter.
- [Samkhya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/philosophies/samkhya): Ancient analytical philosophy distinguishing pure consciousness from material nature.
- [Yoga Darshana](https://www.opensadhaka.com/philosophies/yoga-darshana): Patanjali's systematic path of mental discipline leading to liberation.
- [Mimamsa](https://www.opensadhaka.com/philosophies/mimamsa): Philosophy of Vedic ritual, duty, and the power of sacred action.
- [Nyaya-Vaisheshika](https://www.opensadhaka.com/philosophies/nyaya-vaisheshika): Schools of logic, epistemology, and atomic theory seeking truth through reason.

## Living traditions

- [Shaivism](https://www.opensadhaka.com/traditions/shaivism): Worship of Shiva as the supreme reality, encompassing diverse paths from devotion to tantra.
- [Shaktism](https://www.opensadhaka.com/traditions/shaktism): Worship of the Divine Feminine as the supreme creative power of the universe.
- [Vaishnavism](https://www.opensadhaka.com/traditions/vaishnavism): Devotion to Vishnu and his avatars, especially Rama and Krishna, as the supreme Lord.
- [Smartism](https://www.opensadhaka.com/traditions/smartism): Liberal tradition accepting multiple deities as aspects of one Brahman.
- [Tantra](https://www.opensadhaka.com/traditions/tantra): Esoteric traditions using body, energy, and ritual as vehicles for spiritual transformation.
- [Bhakti Lineages](https://www.opensadhaka.com/traditions/bhakti-lineages): Medieval devotional movements emphasizing love, song, and direct experience of the Divine.
- [Kashmir Shaivism](https://www.opensadhaka.com/traditions/kashmir-shaivism): Non-dual Shaiva philosophy seeing the universe as Shiva's creative self-expression.

## Sacred texts

- [Bhagavad Gita](https://www.opensadhaka.com/texts/bhagavad-gita): The 'Song of the Lord'—Krishna's teaching to Arjuna on dharma, yoga, and liberation.
- [Upanishads](https://www.opensadhaka.com/texts/upanishads): Mystical teachings at the heart of Vedanta, revealing the nature of Brahman and Atman.
- [Yoga Sutras](https://www.opensadhaka.com/texts/yoga-sutras): Patanjali's systematic guide to meditation, mental discipline, and liberation.
- [Devi Mahatmya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/texts/devi-mahatmya): The glory of the Divine Mother—foundational text of Goddess worship.

## Teachers and scholars (Greats)

- [Adi Shankaracharya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/greats/adi-shankaracharya): The 32-year-old philosopher who unified India's spiritual geography and codified non-dualism.
- [Abhinavagupta](https://www.opensadhaka.com/greats/abhinavagupta): The polymath who proved that spiritual liberation and aesthetic rapture are the same phenomenon.
- [Swami Vivekananda](https://www.opensadhaka.com/greats/swami-vivekananda): The first global voice of Sanatan Dharma who bridged the gap between ancient sanyasa and modern life.
- [Sri Aurobindo](https://www.opensadhaka.com/greats/sri-aurobindo): The revolutionary who saw that humanity is not a finished product, but an evolutionary bridge.
- [Kalidasa](https://www.opensadhaka.com/greats/kalidasa): The writer who proved that the most sophisticated art is the shortest path to the most profound truth.

## Practices

- [Japa](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/japa): Repetitive chanting of sacred mantras, often with a mala (prayer beads).
- [Dhyana](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/dhyana): Meditation practice cultivating sustained, focused awareness.
- [Kirtan](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/kirtan): Devotional call-and-response singing of sacred names and hymns.
- [Puja](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/puja): Formal worship ritual honoring the Divine through offerings and ceremony.
- [Seva](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/seva): Selfless service offered as spiritual practice and worship.
- [Svadhyaya](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/svadhyaya): Self-study through sacred texts and introspection.
- [Pranayama](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/pranayama): Breath regulation techniques that harness vital life force (prana) for physical health, mental clarity, and spiritual awakening.
- [Yoga as Sadhana](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/yoga-sadhana): Physical yoga practice as spiritual discipline, not merely exercise.
- [Vrat / Upavasa](https://www.opensadhaka.com/practices/vrat): Sacred fasting and vows as purification and devotional practice.
